column3: Direct parallel: people of the Book are expelled from fortresses after God casts terror into their hearts.
Moses asks God to separate him and his brother from a defiantly corrupt people, echoing the focus's division of a hostile collective.
It portrays rejection of two revelations as mutually supporting magic, but not the focus's overthrow of fortified opponents.
Condemns killing, expulsion, and captive exchange within a divided people; it illuminates the focus's kill-and-capture outcome by contrast.
Within the same siege narrative, a faction seeks to withdraw from the threatened city, setting the military crisis resolved in the focus.
Revelation brought to the Prophet's heart contrasts with terror cast into hostile hearts, but the scenes differ.
Describes diseased hearts worsening in disbelief, a relevant inner condition alongside the terror inflicted on the foes' hearts.
Immediate sequel: the defeated group's land, homes, and wealth pass to the believers after the focus's conquest.
Generic statement that the Quran is a merciful Mighty One's revelation; it does not advance the siege or terror scene.
God casts terror into disbelievers' hearts and commands battle, directly matching the focus's inner terror and combat result.
A later command not to obey unbelievers and hypocrites gives broad chapter context, not the conquest scene.
A people place their clan above God and turn Him aside; this sharpens the focus's account of opponents supported against the Prophet.
Warns believers that obedience to a party of the People of the Book can reverse faith, relevant to the focus's hostile People of the Book.
Thamud divide into two disputing parties, sharing division but not fortification, terror, or conquest.
Warns against turning back after the Messenger's death; only a broad contrast with steadfastness in conflict.
Contrasts unbelievers' arrogant zeal in their hearts with God's tranquility on believers, a useful heart-state parallel.
Mentions a diseased heart in a domestic instruction; only lexical overlap with the focus's hearts.
Truth is cast against falsehood and destroys it, a conceptual parallel to divine force overturning hostile defenses.
A party of the People of the Book conceals known truth, supplying relevant opposition context but no battle scene.
Promise to obedient women in the Prophet's household is unrelated to the focus's military outcome.
Its repeated casting into water is a distinct narrative use of the verb, not the terror cast into hearts.
Nearly repeats the focus's wording: God will cast terror into the hearts of disbelievers because of their associationism.
God casts truth, conceptually resonating with the focus's divine casting, though the object and scene differ.
Believers return unharmed and follow God's pleasure; it offers only general aftermath-of-threat resonance.
Records a recurrent split in Israel's response to messengers: one party denied and another killed them, echoing the focus's divided parties and killing.
Household commands to worship and obey have no material link to the siege and defeat.
Affirms gradual Quranic revelation; the shared descent wording does not illuminate the focus.
Like 2:87, it recounts a party denying and a party killing messengers, a relevant contrast to the focus's divided defeated group.
Opens the same Battle of the Confederates sequence with God's unseen aid against the attacking forces.
Warns against being deceived by unbelievers' movement through lands; it is not connected to the focus's battle.
A party of the People of the Book plots temporary belief and later rejection, giving a relevant pattern of hostile opposition.
The revealed instruction to Moses's mother belongs to a separate casting narrative and adds little.
God sends rain and brings out plants; descent here is unrelated to bringing enemies down.
Sets terms for engagement with the People of the Book, relevant to the identity of the focus's opponents but not its warfare.
Command to remember recited revelations in the Prophet's homes does not clarify the military scene.
Defeated opponents turn back humiliated, a concise parallel to the focus's overthrow of adversaries.
A party of the People of the Book casts God's Book behind their backs, furnishing a relevant pattern of rejection.
Rules on the Prophet's priority and kinship do not materially illuminate the focus.
The Book is cast to the Prophet and he is told not to support disbelievers; only broad opposition context is shared.
Names disbelievers among the People of the Book, matching the focus's opponent category without its event pattern.
A group professes obedience then turns away, a useful parallel to internal withdrawal and divided allegiance.
The sleepers inspire terror in an observer, but it is neither divine battlefield terror nor a hostile collective's collapse.
Identifies disbelievers among the People of the Book awaiting decisive proof, relevant only to the focus's named group.
Instruction on outer garments and protection is unrelated to the defeat of the fortified group.
Generic statement that the Quran is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.
God sends the Book in truth and earlier scriptures; it provides scripture context for the People of the Book, not the battle.
Same siege sequence: fear reaches hearts and believers face the surrounding confederate assault before the focus's resolution.
Generic description of revelation from the Creator does not bear on the focus.
A party of believers resists Satan while others follow him; only a general divided-group pattern.
Etiquette around the Prophet's homes is unrelated to the fortresses and conquest in the focus.
Casting ornaments in the golden-calf episode is a different action and adds no useful relation.
Describes covenant-breaking foes whose mouths and hearts diverge, relevant hostile-heart context without the focus's outcome.
Rejects false social and legal identities; its wordplay on support is not a meaningful bridge to the battle.
Objectors demand an angel be sent down with the Messenger; this is unrelated to the focus.
Commands fighting oath-breakers who sought to expel the Messenger, strongly contextualizing the conflict with treacherous enemies.
Salih rebukes his people for demanding evil; only the neighboring dispute sequence has a faint relation.
Contrasts faith loved in believers' hearts with disbelief hated there; a broad heart-state parallel only.
The Furqan distinguishes truth while disbelievers face severe punishment, broadly consonant with divine judgment on hostile rejecters.
God's knowledge of what is hidden or disclosed does not clarify the conquest scene.
God sees the Prophet's movement among worshippers; it has no relevant connection.
God exposes rancor hidden in diseased hearts, illuminating the inward hostility underlying the focus's terror-struck hearts.
The trust offered to creation is unrelated to the battle and its aftermath.
Contrasts faithful and rebellious followers in a later community; only a general group-division resonance.
Calls for fighting to rescue the oppressed from a town ruled by wrongdoers, broadly related to conflict against oppressive inhabitants.
Truth arrives and falsehood cannot originate or return, a conceptual counterpart to the collapse of hostile power.
Calls the disbeliever a supporter against his Lord; it shares the support root but not the focus's event.
Rejects selective belief in God's revelation and recalls killing prophets, relevant to the focus's hostile People of the Book by contrast.
Rules on whom the Prophet's wives may see are unrelated to the focus.
Clear verses are sent down for guidance; generic revelation language does not aid the battle reading.
Revealed scripture judges disputes and guides believers amid disagreement, a broad parallel to divinely resolving divided communities.
Same battle context: hypocrites are terrified when fear comes and their failed loyalty is exposed.
Divine sending down is central, but it contributes only a distant lexical contrast to God bringing opponents down.
Addresses captives held by the Prophet and locates possible good in their hearts, directly extending the focus's captive outcome.
A stolen hearing is pursued by a piercing flame; only a remote projectile motif overlaps.
A fragmentary reference to what was sent down on the dividers lacks a usable connection to the focus.
The burden that weighed on the Prophet's back is unrelated to hostile support or fortresses.
Rebellious listeners are cast away from every side; the casting motif is distinct from terror in hearts.
Deniers claim the Merciful sent down nothing, offering only general rejection of revelation.
A plotting party cannot mislead the Prophet and God sends him the Book; it gives broad opposition context only.
On judgment day God repays the true debt; no specific link to the focus's earthly conflict.
A surah is sent down with clear ordinances; generic descent does not illuminate the focus.
Receiving a record behind one's back shares a posture word only, not a substantive scene.
Hearts immersed in heedlessness and other deeds provide a relevant inward-obstruction parallel, though no terror or conquest occurs.
Clear verses are sent down and only the defiantly disobedient reject them; generic revelation-rejection context.
Regulates taking captives after forcefully prevailing in battle, directly relevant to the focus's captive party.
The Quran descends upon the Prophet's heart, contrasting divine guidance to a receptive heart with terror in hostile hearts.
Feeding a captive shows the post-capture ethical horizon, relevant to the focus's mention of captives.
Refusal to follow what God sent down shows entrenched inherited resistance, a broad contrast to the focus's defeated opponents.
Disbelievers hurl conjecture about the unseen from afar; only a nonparallel casting verb overlaps.
A sound heart is the positive counterpart to the terror-stricken or diseased hostile heart in the focus.
Thamud carve secure houses in mountains, a useful image of seemingly strong dwellings vulnerable to divine judgment.
Those left behind speak differently from what is in their hearts, shedding light on concealed hostility and fear.
The fading-world parable uses rain sent down and does not materially connect to the focus.
An overwhelming sign could force bowed necks, a limited divine-compulsion parallel but not the focus's battle.
Detailed debt documentation and witness rules are unrelated to the focus.
Rejecters claim they would have followed a sent-down Book, then turn from clear signs; it adds a People-of-the-Book rejection pattern.
Forbids following Satan's steps and mentions purification; it has no specific tie to the focus.
Even collective mutual support cannot reproduce the Quran, a contrast to the focus's hostile group that supported one another.
Satan's temptation of Adam and his spouse is unrelated to the focus's conquest.
Satanic suggestions test diseased and hardened hearts, relevant to the focus's inward terror but in a different setting.
The immediate preceding resolution of the Confederates siege: God repels the unbelievers in rage and spares believers the fight.
Commands killing, capture, siege, and ambush of hostile treaty-breakers, directly paralleling the focus's combat and captives.
Fighting hostile opponents brings divine punishment through believers' hands, disgrace, victory, and healing for believers' hearts.
Explicitly concerns fighting hostile People of the Book, the opponent group named in the focus.
Recalls believers' earlier vulnerability and fear of being seized before God sheltered and strengthened them, supplying battle-context contrast.
Upon gaining mastery in war, believers are to disperse enemies so those behind them take warning; a direct defeat-and-dispersal parallel.
Preparation of force is meant to terrify God's enemy and the believers' enemy, directly complementing the focus's God-cast terror.
Attributes the decisive throwing in battle to God, furnishing a close divine-agency parallel to terror cast into hearts.
Satan initially emboldens and supports the hostile force, then retreats at battle, contrasting the collapse of its apparent support.
The companion passage states that, absent the decree of exile, the same People of the Book would have been punished in this world.
Explains the transfer of the defeated group's property without mounted battle, clarifying the focus's conquest aftermath.
Regulates distribution of the resulting spoils among the Messenger and vulnerable believers, extending the focus's aftermath.
Orders capture and killing of hostile defectors when they refuse peace, closely matching the focus's divided kill-and-capture result.
Again directs capture and killing of those who offer neither peace nor restraint, a direct legal parallel to the focus's outcome.
Sets penalties for those who wage war against God and His Messenger and spread corruption, including killing and exile.
Explains believers' retreat when the two armies met, providing a close battlefield reversal counterpart.
Depicts fear within the same Confederates setting, as hypocrites dread the enemy coalition's return.
Records the believers' faithful response when they saw the confederate forces, framing the siege before its resolution.
